text: Lessons 20 through 22 proved that Shor's algorithm is mathematically sound and runs in polynomial time. This lesson draws the single most important distinction in the chapter: being correct and polynomial on paper is not the same as being runnable today.

This is settled, published mathematics, not a hopeful claim — Shor's algorithm has even been physically demonstrated on real quantum hardware, successfully factoring small numbers like 15 and 21. Those demonstrations prove the algorithm works exactly as described. What they do not prove is that scaling the same approach up to RSA-2048 is currently achievable, because the resource requirements scale very differently from those small toy cases.

A widely cited 2019 analysis by Craig Gidney and Martin Ekerå, titled how to factor 2048 bit RSA integers in 8 hours using 20 million noisy qubits, estimated exactly that: roughly 20 million noisy physical qubits, running for about 8 hours, to factor a single RSA-2048 modulus. That's a specific, peer-reviewed engineering estimate from the published literature, not a figure invented for this lesson.

Real quantum computers built in the 2024 to 2026 era have qubit counts in the tens to low thousands — several orders of magnitude short of that 20 million estimate. And those physical qubits are noisy: building one reliable, error-corrected logical qubit commonly needs hundreds to thousands of physical qubits. Both gaps, raw count and reliability, compound rather than offsetting each other. So it's equally wrong to say Shor's algorithm doesn't really work, and to say RSA is already broken or about to be — the algorithm is proven; the hardware gap is the real, long-term engineering obstacle.
Next lesson explains why the cryptography world is migrating away from RSA anyway, even while today's math says breaking it isn't practical yet.
